utterances.text: Yep. On the third paragraph of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, thank you very much. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you attend this meeting on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is this a short question? Because it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I mean, this will be more or less the last topic, Your Honours, so we could deal with it after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean, I'm happy to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And you will wind up shortly after that because your two hours has been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the other meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Recess taken at 12.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will allow Ms. Korner ten minutes to wrap up. But before she resumes: We're looking at the rest of the day, and I believe that counsel would have all been alerted to the effects of the technical problems that we have. And bearing in mind those realities, in the context of the reasons why the present witness's testimony is being taken by videolink and also the disabilities, for want of a better word, that the accused have from extended sittings, are Defence counsel in the position to indicate how the rest of today could go, in terms of the time they have left and whether this witness could be finished within the compass of today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not sure when Ms. Korner will finish. It is -- it is my assumption that -- that based on how it works -- the communications system works now, that I would need somewhere in -- around two hours for cross-examination of this witness. It is, however -- we are told by the Registrar that the witness is very concerned that he would like to finish before the -- before the weekend. So today and tomorrow. We share that. So in -- in light of the situation that we -- that we had this morning with the communication problem, I'm wondering maybe it would be wise that we -- that we add another session this afternoon, one session this afternoon, and then -- and then -- and then continue -- yes, then continue tomorrow. In that case, we will hundred per cent be sure that we can finish. Because I'm thinking about the telecommunications problems that might develop overnight, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That was the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We were alerted to that by the Registry, and I assume that counsel, too, had been alerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand. And, Your Honours, we can -- depends on the witness, because it is our understanding that he has a health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That was the second thing to which I alluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Which we will -- we are perfectly fine in working the rest of the afternoon and finishing probably even today. I mean, if that is okay with the witness and everybody else, that is, of course, because we have the interpreters, the staff and -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to -- I certainly have no objection, subject to the witness's consent to sitting an extra session. Your Honours, I do want to raise this morning, for various administrative reasons, Your Honours' decision of yesterday, written decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh, I haven't forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it's whether I would -- whether it would assist -- whether we are going to have to sit the whole day. Or at least I would like to deal with that before the next adjournment so that we can make -- I can make the relevant arrangements. And if we have to sit the rest of the day with this witness, then I need to make arrangements fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Okay, so you've answered the last question I was about to raise. In other words, even if we are doing an extended session this afternoon, your issue we would still deal with at the end of this session, rather than waiting until the end of today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all my only concern is, as to whether we sit the whole time. Your Honours, as far as I'm aware, the weather conditions are supposed to be improving again. And if it's one session this afternoon, that's fine. And then continue tomorrow morning to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That works for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I share the views of my colleague Zecevic and my learned friend from the Prosecution. So that's no objection. I have only one session for this witness, so that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just wondered whether Your Honours wanted to check with the witness if he was happy that we continued this afternoon, before I went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll inquire now. I don't know how much of the exchange that has just passed between counsel and the Bench you would have heard, sir, but the -- you remember this morning that there was a delay because of the technical difficulties caused by weather, and we are mindful of your health concerns. And what it now looks like is that when we break for the -- at the end of this session at - well, it wouldn't be 1.45 it would be 1.30 - what we are new thinking about is resuming at 2.45 and sitting for a further hour today, with a view to resuming tomorrow morning. And we are wondering whether that would cause personal difficulties for you, that extra hour this afternoon from 2.45 to 3.45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I will be able to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, when we adjourned, I was just about to ask you about the second meeting which you agree Mico Stanisic did attend. And was that meeting between the -- the two reports, or after the report -- both reports had been delivered to the minister?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I think it was the meeting between these two reports because we can see that from what it says here. And I remember that he attended the meeting now, in view of the criticisms that were sent to the individual members of that inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Where did that meeting take place? In Sarajevo or in Banja Luka? Or Pale, I should say, probably - Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, that was on Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So does that mean that you -- between those -- that you interrupted your inspection of Banja Luka and went back to Pale, had the meeting, and then returned to do the second report?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: A part of those affairs were -- was completed. The report sent in. I assume the minister looked at it, looked at all the reports had that were compiled, and then we returned into the field to continue the job of disbanding the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, in that first report you had mentioned the fact that there were these camps that were being run in Prijedor, according to the information that you had had from Drljaca, of Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje. Did the minister raise the question of those camps with you?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, there was no mention of that at the meeting. No mention of the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So what did the minister say about your report then?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that is. No instructions about the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So what were the further instructions that you were being given?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what was the purpose of the meeting, then, with the minister?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, to go to the centre to look at the quality of the reports. Who had done what, pursuant to the minister's orders. And to move towards disbanding the special police, the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So nothing's said about your report on the -- the camps and the use of the police for security -- for securing the camps. Did he say anything about Mr. Stojan Zupljanin's request for a further explanation of the word "removed"?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, there was no mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. That's all I want to ask you, then, about that --

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Because I was sufficiently clear at the meeting when I said what "removed" meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you actually asked in your report for a dispatch confirming that you were right in your understanding. Did you ever get a dispatch, or was there any verbal confirmation from Mico Stanisic that "removed" did mean "sack"?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any communication between the centre and the ministry on that issue. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's all I ask in that report. Your Honours have admitted -- allowed it to be added to the 65 ter; could it now be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting with the minister, were people present who had carried out inspections or -- inspections for the purposes of implementation of the order in other areas?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think all of them were present. I don't remember whether some individual might have been absent, but mostly everybody who was engaged in that inspection was there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now I would like you to have a look, please, at document which is at tab 11, 10395.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours will see it's not on our 65 ter list. It was the subject of an application in April of this year with a large number of other documents. And it's right to say that Your Honours' ruling on this document was that the 23 documents -- "The Prosecution does not indicate the reasons for their late addition beyond asserting they are relevant to the case." Your Honours, I'm going to ask him about it in the hopes of showing Your Honours why it is relevant, if he can assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see that document there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Cedo Tosic?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know Mr. Vojin Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they, those two inspectors, present at this meeting that you had with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember them. But probably, according to this report, they should have been present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: But I can't remember seeing them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were all the reports that had been submitted - clearly all these inspections had been done in the beginning of August - discussed at this meeting with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the reports that were discussed. It's just if the minister had some comments to make with respect to some specific report. And unless I'm mistaken, it was a report that referred to the Doboj Centre. He had some observations to make, that something was not done properly, that the inspection wasn't done properly. But as to some specific reports and their contents, no, that was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever have sight of the report that was done on the Trebinje area, which covered, amongst other places, Bileca and Gacko, that was prepared by Mr. Cedo Tosic and Mr. Vojin Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have it. I didn't have an insight into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, well, I can't take this matter any further then. Thank you. All right. Then the -- the final document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just check my note for a moment. No, I don't think I need that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Gajic, have any further input into what happened as a result of the report that you produced on Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, I had no further information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And was that the last inspection that you did?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gajic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gajic. My name is Slobodan Zecevic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said at the beginning of your testimony today that in the SUP -- or, rather, the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the war, that you dealt with defence preparations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the legal ground -- foundations for these defence preparations and affairs related to that. Did that stem from the federal Law on Total National Defence and Social Self-Protection which was in force on the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's also a fact, is it not, that the law, that law, governing total national defence or All People's Defence and social self-protection -- yes, go ahead. What were you saying?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Some provisions ... some provisions stemmed from the law governing internal affairs and governmental decisions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But the basic groundwork for defence preparations was the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, as it was called; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that that Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection provided for the fact that all subjects, all institutions, all economic organisations should conduct defence preparations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, sir, it is a fact, is it not, that in October -- or, rather, September 1991, an order from minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, based on the decision taken by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, stated that the reserve police force was mobilised in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember. And it depended on the district stations, how many people were mobilised. It differed from one area to another, how much of the reserve force was to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you will remember that there were comments and objections made to the fact that according to the provisions in force at the time, the government stipulated the provisions of the total number of reserve policemen; whereas, in this case, the Presidency decision was a sweeping, blanket decision and given in September of 1991 and opened up the possibility for taking in persons into the regular reserve force who, according to their qualities, didn't really deserve to be there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: The government decision of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was taken, and it determined -- it spoke about 64.000 members of active -- the active force and reserve force, and special criteria were set which had to be compiled with by those individuals. However, there was a total devaluation of criteria, if I can put it that way, so that nobody knew who became part of the reserve force anymore and who engaged whom on what basis and things like that. So there was no -- there were no criteria anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we agree on that score. Now I'd like to show you a document. It is 1D130, which is tab 12. It's a document dated the 26th of September, 1991. And would you please take a look at page 2 of the document because I'd like us to comment on the number of reserve policemen, the total number of reserve policemen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in actual fact. Can you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There's mention there of the decision taken by the Executive Council, or, rather, the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 23rd of December, 1998 [as interpreted], and it says that it is stipulated that in the republic that there are 33.000 policemen; 6.000 active ones and 27.000 reserve force. Now, I'm just showing you this because in your previous answer you said 63.000, so I'd like to take this opportunity to refresh your memory and to ask you whether you agree that the number was actually 60 -- is 33.000, and not 63.000?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I misspoke. A slip of the tongue. I know that there were 6.000 active-duty ones and the 27.000 others. So I apologise to Their Honours for my interpretation of that. But, yes, 33.000 is the correct figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 35, line 17, of the transcript I said the 23rd of December, "1988," whereas it was recorded "1998," which is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, thank you for that answer in clearing that point up. And I'd like to show you document 1D1257 next, please, which is tab 20. And I'm showing you this document because it was MFI'd. So take a look at the document. I don't know whether you've familiar with it. It's dated 8th of April, 1992, and it refers to a Ministry of Defence dispatch signed by Mr. Osman Jasarevic, on behalf the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D257 is the number, and it's MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just reading the document, the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 20, by the way, in the Defence bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I haven't got ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know Mr. Osman Jasarevic? And if you can tell us who he was.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I do know who he was, but he came to the fore in that pre -- in those pre-war days. I don't know what post he was appointed to. But I do remember the name; I do remember Jasarevic. I think he came from one of the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, he worked in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at its headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of seeing this document before? Have you already seen it?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Thank you. Now, sir, --

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: When data comes -- look -- when looking at data for defence preparations, I never saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that the document bears the date 8th of April; is that correct? At the time, did you go to work at the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Actually, I wasn't in the MUP then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Slobodan [as interpreted] Jasarevic was the chief of a department in the B&H MUP?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: He did have a management function, a post, but I cannot recall what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In response to the Prosecutor's question today at the beginning of your testimony, you said that sometime in early May you moved to the MUP of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you explained that when you arrived you spoke with the chief of the public security service, the under-secretary for public security, Mr. Cedo Kljajic, and that he appointed you as head or chief of defence preparations, so more or less to a similar post where you worked in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Responding to a question by my learned friend Ms. Korner earlier today, I think you gave an answer that was not recorded in the transcript; I believe probably because the connection is bad. I think, if I remember, Ms. Korner asked you if, besides defence preparations, you were also dealing with other matters; and you said, At the time, in the Republika Srpska MUP, defence preparation jobs did not come to the forefront, so I was also writing dispatches and similar things. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said "they did not come to the forefront," these defence preparation jobs, can you very briefly explain what you meant when you said that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: These were tasks transferred from that period and that Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the organisation of the police or the militia or their expert professional training or the principle of procurement with materiel and equipment were not being dealt with. These are some basic principles that should have been applied in carrying out these assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, these defence preparations assignments were just transferred and you were duty-bound to implement them, but due to the conditions that were in the MUP of Republika Srpska at the time, nothing particular was done regarding those matters? I assume that that would be a simplified version of your answer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't really work on those jobs. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you a document from the 15th of May, 1992. This is 1D46, tab 1. This decision, as we can see from the text, is adopted pursuant to the declaration of the imminent threat of war in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the appropriate organisations of the police in that sense. Do you remember this order?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I cannot really remember because I came in early May, so I don't remember. This was at the time when I arrived, so perhaps this order was sent out before I was actually assigned to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then if you're not familiar with it, I'm not going to ask you about it. I would only ask you this generally, if you know, and you did talk about this a little bit with Ms. Korner. It's a question of resubordination of the police in the execution of military tasks to the military. Do you remember speaking about this question?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this order, there is a sentence that was a little bit controversial, so perhaps you can help us about that. Paragraph marked with the number 7 in this order speaks about members of the MUP being resubordinated to the armed forces. And it also -- it says that the ministry of -- units are under the command of ministry officials. So I'm going to ask you this: In a situation when the corps commander requests a certain number of MUP personnel to be resubordinated to a certain military unit, those MUP members go to that assignment in an organised manner. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Namely, when a group of policemen go with the assignment to be resubordinated to a specific military unit, that group of policemen is led by a senior officer who is their commander as well?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That group of policemen is organised within a certain formation, a squad, a company, a battalion, a platoon, and it is under the command of the senior officer from that station or centre; but the entire unit, then, is resubordinated to that particular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. So let's clarify: This leader, senior officer from the public security station or the centre who is leading this police unit, at the time when they reached the military unit to which they are being resubordinated, he reports to the commander of that military unit, and then he and all of the members of the MUP unit are resubordinated to the military command and they become part of the military command structure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While they are executing this assignment, those MUP members, together with their senior officer, are exempted from the MUP command structure and find themselves within the military command structure and are treated as members of military units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That is how it is regulated under the law, and that is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, a typical question at this point would be to ask the witness how it then worked in practice, because it is well enough to be told how things should work according to the rules; often quite another thing is how it worked in practice. But if you bring this issue back to the witness, could you then also inquire to whom the MUP commander who was commanding this unit that would have been resubordinated, to whom did the commander, the MUP commander, report back, if anything happened during the assignments and the resubordination to the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, there's a -- I mean, I was actually on my feet as Your Honour interrupted on the same -- or more or less the same point. Question as put is. "... those MUP members, together with their senior officer, are exempted from the MUP command structure ..." What does that mean? I mean, the witness has said this is how it's regulated under the law. Well, at the moment, I have no idea what the question means nor what law the witness is -- is referring to. I can deal with it in re-examination, but as Your Honours interrupted, I think this ought to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, as can you see, it is still controversial, this matter. The question -- we can -- let's try to explain. At the point when the senior officer, with his unit, is resubordinated to the military unit, those police members, at that point in time, become members of the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And they and their superior officer report and are responsible for their actions to their superior military officers during the time of their resubordination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, When you said that this was so according to the law, are you stating or do you have information to the effect that, in practice, things happened somewhat differently from what you have just confirmed was in accordance with the law and what I said was in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, this is the problem: Which law? Mr. Zecevic isn't specifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have the information as much as -- of it as it reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, continue answering, and then I will put another question.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't have information that there was some kind of dual or parallel command that the superior officer of the police unit would report back along the command line to his commander. He was exclusively responsible to the commander of that unit, that military unit, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, suppose a crime was committed by some of the MUP members during the resubordination to the army, then to who would the commanding officer report? Would that be to the military police or to -- back to his own police station from where they were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any violation - and this is something that I assume; I'm not sure, I'm not the most competent person to make these kind of interpretations - but I think any kind of violation of work duties and any commission of a crime would mean that they would be held responsible within their regular composition. So, in that case, the centre or the public security station would be responsible in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Meaning responsible for taking steps to prosecute the perpetrator; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That perpetrators -- measures would need to be immediately -- to be taken against such a perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, according to the Law on All People's Defence, units of the police are resubordinated during execution of military assignments to military units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's a -- that's a -- that's an inaccurate summary. It says combat activity, not military duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when a unit is resubordinated to a military structure, to a military unit thus, you agreed a little bit earlier that they are then assuming the status of members of the military. They're, at that point in time, no longer officials of the Ministry of the Interior but they have the status of soldiers. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: They are executing all orders, executing all orders that are issued by the commander of that military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If they are executing all the orders coming from the commander of that military unit, then they are, of course, responsible to the commander of that military unit for their actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if they commit a crime as members of the military, they would be subject to arrest by the military police, and they would be then processed before the military judicial organs, just like any other soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I am not a lawyer, and I really cannot recall all the laws and regulations. It's been a long time since I did that. But it's logical that it would be like that. I cannot recall all the regulations relating to this particular subject. There are many such regulations, and I cannot say that I can recall all of them right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is seems that this is a convenient point to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- interrupt the testimony of the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. We are going to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. -- no. Mr. Gajic, as you will recall as we discussed earlier today, we are going to take a -- the Court isn't going to adjourn right at this moment because we have a number of procedural matters with which to deal. But you will be stood down as a witness now, and we will resume your testimony in an hour and ten minutes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I completely forgot. It was actually me who proposed that. I'm truly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So you are excused now, to return in an hour and ten minutes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, this refers to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This refers back to the decision that Your Honours -- a written decision of the 14th of July, in which Your Honours say that of the 53 witnesses that we applied to call to cover the adjudicated facts - and I'm looking at paragraph 19 - the Trial Chamber finds it appropriate to permit the Prosecution to call no more than 44. Now, Your Honours, can I just spend a couple of minutes setting out a few matters. First is this: It took the OTP from the 1st of April to the 27th of May when it filed its application to assess which of the rejected or reversed adjudicated facts we needed to call evidence about, and we made a careful selection and we did not call or apply to call evidence about all of them. We went, in the period of that six or seven weeks, further and assessed which witnesses we actually needed to cover the adjudicated facts, which, in our opinion, were vital to the proper presentation of the Prosecution case. Your Honours took from the 27th of May, when we filed, to yesterday to issue the decision, and in the paragraph I've referred to, paragraph 19, say that: "The Trial Chamber has also reviewed whether the anticipated testimony of each proposed witness pertains to the corresponding denied adjudicated facts as indicated by the Prosecution. "On the basis of its analysis," and I highlight the word analysis, "and bearing in mind the balance to be reached between the Prosecution's duty to prove its case and the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial," which matter you dealt with in the simultaneous decision rejecting our leave for our appeal, "and of adequate time for the preparation of the Defence, the Trial Chamber finds it appropriate to permit the Prosecution to call no more than 44 of the witnesses." Now, Your Honours, from that we take it that Your Honours' analysis has indicated that, contrary to what our analysis, we made a mistake, and that we have actually listed nine witnesses who it's unnecessary to call, by Your Honours' only analysis, because they're covered by other witnesses or other evidence. Your Honours actually don't tell us, however, which those witnesses are, because you go on to say that we are ordered to identify the proposed witness it will seek to add to its witness list and the mode of testimony and then say that we have until Monday to do that. Now, Your Honours, we have to -- if we're right and we -- if -- Your Honours, sorry, if you're right and we've made this mistake, you haven't told us where we've made the mistake or what the names of the witnesses are. So we have to do a complete re-analysis of what we -- took us seven weeks to do on the last occasion to sort out where Your Honours' analysis and ours differs. Your Honours give us three days, five including today and the weekend. Now, Your Honours, in fairness to us. And this has, we submit, been a fair -- a question of fairness to the Prosecution throughout, over this whole vexed matter of adjudicated facts, we're asking Your Honours, please, to indicate to us which are the nine witnesses that we need not call so that we can, if necessary, perhaps seek to persuade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Would not that be trespassing -- would not the Trial Chamber then be trespassing on your prerogative if we were to do that? I understand the logic of what you're saying, but wouldn't it be a step too far for the Trial Chamber to presume to tell you which of the 53, on our analysis, which, as you would appreciate, is something that we would have been obliged to conduct notwithstanding the analysis that we appreciate the OTP would have done. Wouldn't it be inappropriate for us to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. Because we've listed in our annex the witnesses and the adjudicated fact to which that witness goes. Your Honours say we're wrong in nine specific cases. And we're saying, at the moment, we need each of those witnesses for each of these selected facts because they are -- they go to the heart, the core, of our case. And you say we're wrong. So we would like to be told where we're wrong, which of the witnesses we don't need, so that we can possibly apply to Your Honours for reconsideration. Because clearly we haven't made the position clear enough. And, Your Honours, at the moment we are in an impossible position, certainly an impossible position, to do this exercise within five days, which took us seven weeks to do last time and which has taken Your Honours much the same time. Therefore, Your Honours, we're asking, if we've made the mistake, then Your Honours should indicate to us which of the witnesses we've made the mistake about so that we can either accept it and do the analysis on a limited basis, or apply to Your Honours for reconsideration. We certainly cannot complete such an exercise in five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If given a longer period, would -- would that assist?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously it will assist, but, Your Honour, we're still saying, but what is the problem - if I may put this in a rhetorical question - about telling us which of the nine witnesses we don't actually need according to Your Honours' analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the Chamber thinks that it would be inappropriate to disclose the analysis that we have made. But what we did, in general terms, was to a apply what we would call a bear-minimum approach; namely, to see which of the witnesses that you had proposed would be necessary to cover the 293 facts or whatever the number is. Or the ones that you had sought to cover only. And that brought us, after having carefully reviewed the matter, to the number of 44 witnesses. This was not an arbitrary number. This was what we -- that was the conclusion that we arrived at after having reviewed the matter. And -- and apart from the reason that has already been offered by the Presiding Judge, namely, that it would be inappropriate for the Chamber to direct the calling of the evidence on behalf of the Prosecution, on top of that, we thought, actually, that we were doing you a favour in allowing you to pick yourself the number -- or the -- the -- individual witnesses among those 53. And, lastly, we understand that it would be maybe difficult for you to -- to do this by Monday. We didn't believe that you would need another seven weeks to -- to review this. But we would be willing to provide you more time, if that would be necessary, and -- because also, in our order, is implied an attempt to reach some sort of -- of an understanding with the Defence teams about which witnesses could be called under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that Mr. Zecevic wants to address you on that part of it. But can I just return to what I originally said. Your Honours, I appreciate that Your Honours are saying you don't think it's right to interfere with the presentation of our case, but, Your Honours, in effect, every decision you make affects the presentation of our case, and you have declined to let us call witnesses, declined on other occasions to let us call documents, and other occasions have let us add -- have let us put in documents. So everything, all your decisions, affect how we present our case. So therefore I'm saying that the simplest thing would be, really the simplest: You've done this analysis. You've said, We don't need these nine witnesses; they are sufficiently covered. The simply thing would be for you to, through your Legal Officers, to notify us who you say those witnesses are. We will then consider the matter. It makes life much quicker, much easier. We'll stick to the deadline of Tuesday -- on Monday, sorry. And we'll deal with it. I mean, we are very anxious to move this case forward, as I know Your Honours are. And, therefore, we don't want to have to spend a lot of time re-analysing, because it has a real effect on our case. If we pick the wrong person or drop or decide we can't cover a particular fact, that has a knock-on effect on what we prove. So, Your Honours, I leave is at that with Your Honours. As far as -- if Your Honours still take the view that you shouldn't, in fairness to the Prosecution, tell us -- tell us who -- where we're gone wrong, then I would simply say we would like until the -- the final day before sitting [sic] to -- to deal with this. We don't want to delay matters any further because, as I say, we are exceedingly anxious, as I know the Court is, to move this case on. Your Honour, the second matter is this, because it affects the second part of your order, which is that we should say how long -- we can't do 92 ter, they have to be viva voce, and we need to give time estimates. And you say the Chamber reiterates the testimony of each selected proposed witness will be admissible solely for the limited purpose of seeking to establish the substance of a specified denied fact. However, we take it that simply doesn't mean, Let's take a fact. Whereas, in fact, Your Honours changed, but we've decided we've covered. For example, Your Honours crossed out the word "detention" from Manjaca, which left us with Manjaca was a camp as an adjudicated fact. We have, in fact, we decided, called sufficient evidence to deal with that. But does this part of Your Honours mean simply that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we are well over -- we are several minutes past the time. Inasmuch as the witness has agreed -- Mr. Gajic has agreed to return for an hour this afternoon, could we pick this up when --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- he would have been released -- excused for the rest of the day. Because you have indicated that Mr. Zecevic wants to be heard on another part of our order, so we will continue this discussion this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Returning at when? 2.45?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 2.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown 1D176, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the order of the 27th of July, 1992, pursuant to which you made an inspection of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2, that's at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's possible -- it actually might be the Prosecution number 2; I'm sorry. Mr. Gajic, do you see this order? Well, you looked at it this morning with my learned friend Ms. Korner. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At page 2, under number 6, the implementation of this order and provision of professional assistance was assigned to some persons so that, for the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Mr. Milos Zuban was tasked with this; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milos Zuban, as the chief of the police affairs in the Republika Srpska MUP, or, rather, in the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was styled at the time, was your immediate superior; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It would be logical to assume, then, that if he was in charge, that he actually delegated the authority to you, the authority, the powers to inspect, visit, and provide professional assistance in the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was logical, but he did not delegate any authority to me. He didn't give me any instructions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Gajic, you knew what your task was, based on this order, and you knew why you were going to Banja Luka, to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, pursuant to this order, to the Security Services Centre, but I assumed that this order, the provisions in this paragraph, actually pertain to a continuous monitoring and provision of professional help. Do you see what I mean? It was meant for a longer period of time, as regards the deployment or assignment of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree, yes. I absolutely agree with you. Because the chief for police affairs, Mr. Milos Zuban, was able to then dispatch his subordinate personnel to visit and inspect those centres that he -- that were in his purview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, tell me, when you left to carry out this task, on both occasions, the first and the second time, because, as we heard from you, you came back at one point, so both times you acted in accordance with instructions you had received from your superiors. You did not do anything on your own initiative, so to speak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: It was absolutely impossible to do anything on one's own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, on that occasion, one of the instructions that you received was to familiarise yourself with the work and any problems that the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka may be experiencing at that time or up to at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like you to look at P631. It's your report, the first report. It's at tab 8; the Prosecution tab 8. The date is the 5th of August. You commented on this document when asked to do so by my colleague. You dealt with some of the issues in this document. You can see at page 1, where it says -- well, this is something that you discussed with Ms. Korner. It -- there is mention of 300 personnel -- police personnel working on providing security of the camps, and then in parentheses, (Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje). Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received this information from the chief of the public security station, Mr. Simo Drljaca. That's the public security station in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the sentence continues, you say that the 300 police personnel are providing security to the camps where prisoners of war are kept. Because this -- well, it's on the same page, page 1. It's the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this information that there were prisoners of war in the camp, did you also receive it from Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that based on what Mr. Drljaca had said, that arrangements been made with officers of the 1st Krajina Corps and the Crisis Staff about the takeover of the security of the camp -- in the camps by the military, that they should take over. And this was also, yet again, something that you heard from Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me --

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Drljaca told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of this conversation in Prijedor, did Mr. Drljaca tell you that various unlawful acts had been done, such as murder, torture, and mistreatment of the persons detained there, and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me anything as regards that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you had had this kind of information, you would have included it in your report, I assume?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Because I put in everything that was available to me, everything that I learned, so I would definitely have put that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this fact that a large number of police personnel provided security in those camps in Prijedor was a serious problem. Because at page 4 of this document you put forward one of your conclusions or proposals. It's in paragraph 7: To urgently contact the army command and to discuss the issue of who was authorised to provide security in the camps in the Prijedor area. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, after you submitted this report, since it is dated the 5th of August, that, on the 6th of August, there was a meeting that you claim was attended by Minister Stanisic, and this meeting was attended by all the employees who had carried out the inspections in the public security -- in the Security Services Centres all over Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your examination, you said that the minister was quite critical, and you recalled that he was specifically critical about the shortcomings in the report as it pertained to the Doboj Security Services Centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think it pertained to the Doboj Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, is it not, that Minister Stanisic and other high-ranking senior personnel in the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina insisted on being given full a full and accurate information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is undoubtedly one of the reasons why the inspectors, including yourself, were dispatched again to the Security Services Centres, in order to amend your reports. My colleague showed to you a report from Trebinje, and it is quite clear and uncontroversial that you went back to Jahorina after this and made another report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In order to supplement it and to complete all the items that were to be dealt with, pursuant to the order of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this was done undoubtedly pursuant to the order and the instructions of the minister?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you mentioned this in your statement, but let me deal with it now. It is true that the position of the ministry, as a whole, headed by the minister and all the other senior personnel was that all the police officers who had committed crimes should be tried, should be prosecuted, or should be sanctioned with disciplinary measures, and should be dismissed from the ministry; and there were orders to that effect. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position of the senior people in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to look at P1502. That's at tab 9. It was 65 ter 10394.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is your second report dated the 10th of August. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At page 2, you report to the ministry - page 2, down below paragraph 5 or item number 5 - you indicated that you had received information that in the Security Services Centre area there were no special or any other units.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the chief of the centre informed you about the problem of the operation of the light brigades that were active in the area covered by the Security Services Centre, Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On this same page, the last paragraph, you say that in the investigations centre in Omarska there are about 175 persons who are secured --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have to move on to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- by 40 police officers from the public security station in Prijedor. I assume that you received this information from the chief of the public security station, Mr. Simo Drljaca. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if Simo Drljaca told me that. I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in this document - this is the document dated the 10th of August - you provide the exact number of persons who are in the investigation centre and the exact number of police personnel securing them. So you must have received that information from somebody who knew that; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This second report, when I drafted it, I did not go to Prijedor. This visit was limited to Banja Luka. So it is possible that one of the associates of Mr. Zupljanin provided this information, because he attended the meeting. And the area of Prijedor, among other areas, was within their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, sir, isn't it, that there was a certain degree of animosity on the part of Mr. Drljaca because he wanted the public security station of Prijedor to actually become a Security Services Centre. Isn't at that so?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: There was a major clash between Mr. Drljaca and -- well, he was probably the one who was the cause of the animosity, and he did not allow the special unit to be deployed in that area and to be engaged in that area. He wanted this to become a centre. And he just wanted to be the boss in that whole area?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He said -- you said that he showed disrespect for the centre and for -- in Banja Luka and for its chief, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, further on --

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: And he insisted that the public security station --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go on. You can finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: He insisted that the public security station be transformed into a Security Services Centre and that he also have a unit, a special unit, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, further down in this text in your report of the 10th of August - in other words, your last report from the CSB in Banja Luka which was forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior - you say that after the investigation was completed, some four to five days later, individuals from Omarska will be transferred to Manjaca, and this investigation centre is to be shut down. I assume that this is information that you received from someone, seeing that you put it in your report?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that the reception centre in Trnopolje was established, that it held individuals of Muslim ethnicity who found refuge and safety there, and that these individual freely could move around, and that this camp was secured by the army and the Red Cross. This is information that you had no reason to doubt, and that is why you put it in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, you say that the so-called Keraterm Camp was shut down and military prisoners were transferred to Manjaca. That, too, is information that you put in your report.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at the very end of this report, you say that the enforcement of other measures contained in the order of the minister of the interior, and, in particular, those measures that pertain to individuals who were criminally -- who had been convicted or who had committed crimes during the war is under way. And then you go on to say that operatives are in the field and they are working on the enforcement on the entire order. These measures mentioned here relate to the prosecution -- or, rather, the implementation and initiation of criminal and disciplinary proceedings against members of police who had actually violated the oath of service and their uniform and the rules of what they did.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you have -- you were a police officer for many years; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean during your career you were a police servant. You served in the police; now you're retired. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you went to conduct an inspection as an inspector of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You toured and carried out an inspection, and you were supposed to report on the situation in the area of the CSB of Banja Luka. You went for the first time in early August, and then your next visit followed a week after. What you put down in the report, you stand by those facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. With full responsibility, I stand by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, your immediate superiors and the Public Security Service had no reason to doubt the truthfulness or accuracy of the report that you submitted; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: It was never suggested to me in any manner that there were some shortcomings in my report. Not on one single occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in 1994, you were still a member of the MUP of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you the annual report of the MUP of Republika Srpska for 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's under tab 14, the Prosecution binder, and the document bears the number 1D03-4465.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the report, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you began your evidence, you will recall that my learned friend Ms. Korner asked you something about the drafting of dispatches and the communication system that existed in the Republika Srpska MUP, and you said that you received replies to your dispatches. Sometimes they were tardy; sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that, according to you, the communication did exist; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, sir, wouldn't you, that the chief of communications and communications assets were Mr. Dragan Kezunovic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can also agree with me, I suppose, that, based on his position and role and his duties, he would be the individuals -- the individual who could provide information on the communications equipment and assets that existed and were used in the Republika Srpska MUP at the time. He would be the best-placed person for that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETO GAJIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you because I'm not really competent in terms of the accuracy and the completeness of the system and how it functioned. And I said that sometimes the communications were tardy. But Mr. Kezunovic is the competent individual who can give you full information on the communications system within the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all its equipment and assets and the way they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Coming back to your reminder, Ms. Korner, on the Ewa Tabeau question: The Chamber is ready to hand down an oral decision on the matter, and then that will be followed up by a written decision, eventually. But in order to speed up response from the Chamber, I will now read out the order that we have agreed on. And it reads as follows: On 29 February 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion pursuant to Rule 94 bis whereby it, inter alia, requested that Ewa Tabeau be considered as a demographics expert and provided a report originally prepared for the Krajisnik case. On 17th August 2009, the Prosecution then filed a supplemental motion, seeking, inter alia, to substitute the Krajisnik report by two new reports. Namely, one, an updated version thereof, prepared for this case; and, two, a report prepared for the Slobodan Milosevic case, which sets out the methodology used and is referenced extensively in the updated Krajisnik report. On 10 March 2010, then, the Prosecution sought to supplement Ewa Tabeau's evidence by a new report. The Prosecution submits that its Demographic Unit undertook: "A more general research exercise into war-related deaths in Bosnia between 1992 and 1995 ... as part of the Completion Strategy and the provision of a legacy of the Tribunal." This exercise was completed in late October 2009. On 12 November, 2009, the Prosecution asked Ewa Tabeau to prepare yet a new report based on this general research exercise. The report was finalised on 18 February 2010 and was then disclosed to Defence on 5th March 2010. Both Defence teams object to the new report, arguing that the Prosecution failed to give a viable explanation to justify why the report was prepared in late 2009. The Trial Chamber has considered the parties' arguments in the relevant submissions and hold that Ewa Tabeau may be considered an expert in demography. It further considers that the updated Krajisnik report and the related report prepared for the Slobodan Milosevic case are relevant to this case. In respect of the last report provided on 10th March 2010, the Trial Chamber holds that the Prosecution didn't act with due diligence in requesting Ewa Tabeau in November 2010 to prepare the report. Moreover, the reasons stated for requesting the new report - that is, the Completion Strategy prompted by -- prompted the undertaking of a general research exercise to provide a legacy of the Tribunal - do not amount to good cause. Nevertheless, the new report is relevant to the present case, and it would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. In view of this fact that this 25-page report was disclosed on 5 March 2010, the Chamber is satisfied that the Defence will not suffer undue prejudice. The Chamber will, therefore, permit Ewa Tabeau to testify regarding these three latest reports. So, in conclusion, Ms. Ewa Tabeau can be called as an expert and we will admit -- we will accept her three latest reports as expert reports. And then we will, by the end of her testimony, take a position, a final position, of which of the three reports or which parts of the three reports will eventually be admitted into the evidence. So that is the ruling. Thank you, Mr. President.
